title: Does an Executable Validator Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM-Generated Network Configuration Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow. Using a deterministic paired design with N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 tasks per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine) we produced a single shared initial candidate per task via gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120) and evaluated the identical candidate under both conditions. A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0) enforced structured workflow policies and could trigger at most one repair iteration per guarded episode. Observed outcomes: baseline success = 120/120; guarded success = 120/120; paired contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap-percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Validator traces report repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We expand methodological detail, execution accounting, representative diagnostics, reproducibility guidance grounded in archived artifacts, and discuss construct/external validity limits and design recommendations for future confirmatory studies.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) promise to translate operator intent into concrete network configuration commands and thereby improve NetOps productivity. However, syntactically plausible command sequences can violate sequencing- and stateful workflow invariants (for example, changing MTU without an enforced shutdown or performing an unsafe uplink switchover), producing semantic failures visible only in closed-loop execution. Prior work recommends integrating verification, emulation, digital twins, or veto layers so generated candidates are validated before enactment; measuring the marginal contribution of such validators requires executable tests that capture stateful, temporal, and group-level invariants rather than token- or syntax-level correctness alone.

We conducted a preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that isolates the marginal effect of an executable emulator validator and a bounded repair policy on identical generator outputs. The confirmatory research question was: Does integrating an executable network emulator as a validator in a generate→validate→repair pipeline reduce semantic/network-level failures when enacting LLM-generated configuration changes compared to an LLM-only suggestion workflow? To isolate validator/repair effects we used a shared-initial-candidate paired design: for each task a single generator output was produced and scored both as baseline (LLM-only) and as guarded (validator±repair). This controls generator-induced variance and addresses a mechanistic question about the validator/repair subsystem itself.
sections.related_work:
Two complementary strands motivate this study. First, emulation- and executable-benchmark research for NetOps emphasizes that text- or token-level correctness does not guarantee safe enactment: closed-loop emulation exposes sequencing and stateful errors—make-before-break mistakes, group-availability violations, and required-ordered operations—that simple syntactic checks miss. Recent executable benchmarks and tool papers (for example, NetConfArena, Benchmarking LLM-Driven Network Configuration Repair, and Aether) provide empirical evidence that closed-loop tests detect errors that static checks overlook [https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23179, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22513, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.18233]. Second, the literature on tool-augmented LLM agents and bounded-autonomy guardrails surveys architectures (veto layers, canaries, generate→validate→repair) proposed to reduce operational risk; these studies argue for runtime verification and for delegating safety-critical checks to deterministic solvers or emulators [see related surveys and architectural reports in the verification and agentic-NetOps literature].

Our study complements prior work by using a shared-generation paired design to isolate validator/repair marginal effects for identical generator outputs. This contrasts with prior generator-focused studies that conflate generator variability with verification efficacy and highlights how different experimental lenses—generator-focused vs validator-focused—affect what inferences are possible.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan. The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1 before any experiment execution. The preregistration specified a paired-binary confirmatory design with N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks partitioned deterministically into three topology classes (edge/core/leaf–spine) with 40 tasks per class. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the prespecified test was the exact two-sided McNemar. A bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) for the paired-difference estimate was included. The preregistration also defined exclusion/contamination rules, a repair budget (≤1 repair per guarded episode), deterministic reset controls, and sensitivity analyses (including treating technical exclusions as failures).

Task generation and structured payload. Tasks were produced deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Each task payload encoded initial_state, expected_final_state, a natural-language intent, a required_sequence (canonical ordered operations), and difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, required_command_count, level). Required_sequence and workflow_policies were explicit structured constraints (examples: must_be_down_for_fields, final_group_constraints, make-before-break patterns) that the emulator validator enforces as executable checks rather than as heuristic text matches.

Shared-generation paired design and rationale. For each paired task we issued a single shared initial generation call to the declared hosted model (gpt-5-mini) and recorded the shared candidate. The identical shared candidate was then scored in both the baseline and guarded conditions; model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair) while the planned maximum_model_calls = 240. This design removes generator variance across paired episodes and cleanly attributes any paired discordance to validator or repair actions. A recognized trade-off is that when the generator produces valid candidates for the chosen task bank the validator cannot exercise repair; this trade-off was explicit in the preregistration.

Validator and repair semantics. The guarded pipeline invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0), an executable state checker that (a) executes the shared candidate in an emulator of initial_state, (b) enforces workflow_policies encoded in the task payload, and (c) emits a structured validator_trace that records validation_before, validation_after, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_count, violation_codes, and an explicit repair_applied boolean. The preregistered repair policy permitted at most one repair iteration when validator.violation_count > 0; repair prompts and any provider traces would be archived. In this execution validator.violation_count = 0 for all guarded episodes and repair_applied = false in every validator_trace.

Instrumentation, contamination controls, and deterministic reconciliation. The harness enforced deterministic emulator resets between tasks, container checksum verification, and provider-call audit trails (hosted_model_call_event_count = 120; cache_hit_count = 0; cache_miss_count = 120). Contamination heuristics included duplicate-output detection and cross-condition cache-key reuse detection; none were triggered. Deterministic reconciliation confirmed pair accounting and provider-audit consistency (complete_pair_count = 120; planned_episode_count = 240; completed_episode_count = 240; failed_episode_count = 0).

Scoring and outcome definitions. Each paired episode produced a binary semantic outcome: pass (semantic_success = 1) when the emulator-observed final_state satisfied the task's expected_final_state and required_sequence constraints, and fail (semantic_success = 0) otherwise. The deterministic validator also produced a score_reason_code (e.g., VALID_CONFIGURATION). All scoring followed the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation rule implemented by the validator.
sections.results:
Execution summary and primary outcome. The run completed without technical exclusions. Condition-level summaries: baseline successes = 120, baseline failures = 0; guarded successes = 120, guarded failures = 0 (success rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table: n_11 = 120, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Exact two-sided McNemar p-value = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00. Bootstrap-percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Validator traces report repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; therefore no repair-provider-call artifacts exist.

Per-topology outcomes. The preregistered deterministic partition produced 40 tasks per topology class. Per-topology counts were:
- Edge (40 tasks): baseline = 40/40 success; guarded = 40/40 success.
- Core (40 tasks): baseline = 40/40 success; guarded = 40/40 success.
- Leaf–spine (40 tasks): baseline = 40/40 success; guarded = 40/40 success.

Representative diagnostics. Representative scoring and validator traces in the archived artifacts show that for sampled tasks normalized_response equaled normalized_reference_answer, parsed_command_count matched required_command_count from the task payload, validator.validation_after.valid = true, and validator.repair_applied = false. Representative task payloads include required_sequence entries such as shutdown→configure→restore and make-before-break uplink switchover; archived validator traces show these canonical constraints were satisfied by generator outputs under the frozen prompt strategy. Example artifact excerpts (archived) include observed_touched_field_count values and difficulty metadata (level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}) for representative tasks, confirming that the harness exercised a range of policy-complexity motifs even though no semantic violations occurred.

Repair activity and secondary endpoints. Because validator.violation_count = 0 across the run, no repairs were applied and secondary endpoints quantifying repair incidence are vacuous in this execution. This absence is an empirical observation recorded in validator traces and in the deterministic reconciliation artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome. The paired shared-generation design was chosen to answer a narrowly scoped mechanistic question—can a validator/repair subsystem improve outcomes for identical generator outputs? In the archived task bank and under the declared generator/prompt configuration the single shared initial candidates satisfied the deterministic emulator validator in all 120 pairs; consequently the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to exercise repair and could not reduce semantic failures relative to the baseline. The exact McNemar p = 1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00] are statistical expressions of this ceiling outcome: with zero discordant pairs all resamples reproduce the same paired table, so the percentile bootstrap CI is necessarily degenerate under the preregistered resampling scheme.

Design trade-offs and recommendations. The shared-generation protocol increases internal validity for isolating validator effects but may under-exercise repair when the generator is well-calibrated for the chosen task bank. Based on recorded task-manifest difficulty metadata and the absence of repairs, practical preregistered adjustments for future confirmatory runs include:
1) Independent generation per condition: permit separate generator draws per condition and account for additional variance in the analysis so guarded pipelines can intercept generator errors arising from prompt or sampling variability.
2) Controlled prompt perturbations: prespecify perturbation variants (for example, two perturbation variants per task) on a subset of tasks to increase generator error incidence while preserving other paired blocks for internal control.
3) Task stratification toward high-complexity cases: concentrate power on tasks labeled 'very_hard' or with higher dependency_rule_count and required_command_count to increase the probability of generator-induced violations and thereby exercise repair behavior.
4) Expanded repair budget in exploratory arms: allow more than one repair iteration in exploratory arms to observe repair convergence dynamics and repair-call costs.

Operational implications and auditability. Even when unused, a deterministic validator that emits structured traces (checked rules, touched fields, and explicit repair flags) supports operator auditability, post-hoc diagnosis, and compliance reporting. Instrumented accounting (provider-call audits, scoring traces, deterministic reconciliation) supports operator-facing explanations and third-party audit processes in deployments where generators sometimes err. The experiment underlines that claims about repair benefits require careful experimental framing: if generators rarely produce invalid candidates under a frozen prompt, the guard will be idle by design.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is strong in this run: deterministic provisioning, exhaustive provider-call audits, zero exclusions, and reproducible validator traces. Construct validity is limited by the validator's policy encodings derived from synthetic task payloads; while required_sequence enforces canonical workflows the validator does not emulate every vendor-specific behavior or telemetry partial-observability. External validity is constrained by the synthetic deterministic task corpus, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy. Conclusion validity is affected by the statistical ceiling: the preregistered power calculation assumed baseline failure ≈ 0.40 and targeted an absolute reduction of 0.15; observed baseline = 0.00 violates those assumptions and makes the confirmatory McNemar test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size. These validity assessments are grounded in the preregistration, execution accounting, and deterministic reconciliation artifacts archived with the run.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline against an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness with a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, yielding n_11 = 120 and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The result documents a ceiling for this curated synthetic task bank and illustrates that a shared-generation paired design can mask repair benefits that would appear if generators sometimes produce invalid candidates. Our principal scientific contribution is methodological: we show how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and how deterministic archival artifacts (task manifests, validator traces, provider-call audits, and reconciliation files) enable reproducible failure analysis and transparent auditing even when the primary confirmatory test is degenerate. The archived artifacts permit follow-up studies that relax the shared-generation constraint, compare generator families, expand repair budgets, and evaluate more production-rooted corpora to quantify practical repair utility under realistic generator variance.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for demonstrating the preregistered effect size.
